title: Show a critical awareness of language usage

lessons.title: Language has a purpose
lessons.html:
Why we use language

Every time people speak or write, they want something. They want to inform (give facts), persuade (make you believe or buy something), instruct (tell you what to do), or entertain. Being critically aware means asking: Who is speaking? What do they want? Is it true? Is it fair?

Examples from daily life

TextMain purpose
A label on a chemical containerInstruct and warn
A poster for cheap cellphone dataPersuade
A notice about a farm meetingInform
A radio dramaEntertain

Fact and opinion

A fact can be checked and proved, for example: The meeting is on Friday at 10:00 in the shed. An opinion is what someone thinks or feels, for example: This is the best tractor in South Africa. Opinions are not wrong, but you should not treat them as facts.

Persuasive language

Advertisements and some people use tricks to make you agree:

  • Big promises: Get rich in one week!
  • Pressure: Only today! Last chance!
  • Famous people saying they use a product.
  • Strong emotional words: amazing, miracle, guaranteed.

When you hear words like these, slow down and ask questions. If something sounds too good to be true, it usually is. Many scams on WhatsApp and SMS use exactly these tricks to get your money or your bank details.

Tone

The same message can be said in a kind way or a rude way. The words, voice and body language we choose show our attitude, and affect how people respond.

lessons.title: Respectful and fair language
lessons.html:
Words can hurt or help

Language can bring people together or push them apart. South Africa has 12 official languages, including South African Sign Language, and many cultures. At work on a farm, people from different backgrounds work side by side. The way we speak to each other matters.

Unfair or biased language

  • Racist language: insulting names for people of a certain race. This is hurtful and can be against the law.
  • Sexist language: words that put down women or men, for example saying a job is only for men. Women drive tractors and manage farms; men cook and care for children.
  • Stereotypes: saying all people from one group are the same, for example all young people are lazy.
  • Insulting people with disabilities by using cruel names.

Such language is disrespectful and can lead to conflict, discipline at work or even legal action.

Choosing better words

Instead ofSay
Hey you, boy!Use the person's name
Chairman (for any person)Chairperson
That disabled guyOur colleague who uses a wheelchair, or his name

Language and power

Sometimes people use difficult words or a language others do not understand to keep information from them. For example, a contract in a language a worker cannot read. You have the right to ask for an explanation in a language you understand. If a document is unclear, ask questions before you sign or agree.

Listening critically

When you hear news, rumours or messages, ask: Who said this? How do they know? Is there proof? Do not forward messages you have not checked. Fake news can cause panic and harm.

Key points

  • Language is used to inform, persuade, instruct or entertain.
  • Facts can be proved; opinions are what people think.
  • Watch for persuasive tricks and scams that sound too good to be true.
  • Avoid racist, sexist and stereotyping language.
  • Ask for explanations in a language you understand, and check before you share.
